A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MedRAX and ChestAgentBench, with readable text, figures, tables, and algorithms. v1 ends with references; v2 adds Appendices A and B. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on ChestAgentBench and CheXbench in Tables 1–2, alongside clinical case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains those original evaluations and adds MedRAX results for MIMIC-CXR report generation and a separate SLAKE evaluation. Comparator scores in the new tables are explicitly attributed to prior literature.

M1.justification: The ReAct agent, backbone, and specialized toolbox remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 replaces single-tool execution with explicit parallel tool calls, but v1 Section 3.2 already describes parallel execution. Appendix A expands documentation rather than establishing a newly introduced method component.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluation of single-image radiology report generation on MIMIC-CXR, substantially extending the evaluated tasks beyond question answering and image-text reasoning. Existing ChestAgentBench and CheXbench coverage remains. The additional SLAKE experiment uses an existing dataset and chest-X-ray VQA task under another evaluation selection.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their comparator sets. New Table 3 compares against CheXagent, MAIRA-1, LLaVA-Rad, Med-PaLM M 84B, and M4CXR; Table 4 includes RadFM, CheXagent, and M4CXR. These substantially expand the reported comparisons, with the new tables explicitly sourcing baseline scores from Park et al.

E3.justification: New protocols evaluate 3,858 MIMIC-CXR test images using CheXbert micro- and macro-F1 over 14 and five labels, and 114 English closed-ended SLAKE chest-X-ray samples using exact-match accuracy and word recall. These supplement the retained evaluations rather than revise their settings. The newly specified GPT-4o quality checks do not establish that ChestAgentBench was rebuilt.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds a descriptive analysis of benchmark composition across clinical settings and 20 pathological findings, extending v1's demographic and anatomical summaries. Figure 2 also revises the worked grounding/segmentation example. The two Section 5.4 diagnostic case studies remain, and no controlled ablation or measured robustness test is added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2 adds point scores and descriptive case frequencies without changing uncertainty-reporting practices; the demographic standard deviation in Figure 3 is retained.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 are numerically unchanged. New Table 3 reports MedRAX micro-F1 scores of 79.1/64.9 and macro-F1 scores of 34.2/48.2. Table 4 adds 90.35% accuracy and 91.23% recall on the separate SLAKE selection; these do not replace the retained 82.9% SLAKE result. Appendix B adds case-frequency results, and Figure 2 revises illustrative tool outputs.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. Appendix A explains the existing algorithm and memory updates without introducing substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same claims: training-free orchestration of specialized CXR tools, the 2,500-question ChestAgentBench, superior benchmark performance, and a deployable interface. The additional evaluations support these existing claims rather than redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets stronger micro-F1 but weaker macro-F1 as suggesting better performance on prevalent conditions. Its future-work discussion additionally identifies error propagation and spurious correlations in pretrained models. Existing limitations concerning conflicting tool outputs, computational overhead, and missing uncertainty quantification remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly supplies the system prompt, tool-wrapper fields, message construction, argument validation, memory handling, failure recovery, and orchestration details. Section 4.2 specifies automated GPT-4o quality verification. The Impact Statement adds licensing information and reports Azure OpenAI use with logging disabled. These substantially expand documentation without establishing changes to the underlying implementation.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of RaDialog, M4CXR, and AgentClinic, plus citations supporting the new comparisons and other background statements. The central positioning as a specialized, training-free CXR agent remains unchanged; the related-work expansion is limited rather than a conceptual repositioning.

P1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands the terse algorithm description into a structured explanation of components and execution stages. v2 also adds an Impact Statement and benchmark-statistics appendix, condenses introduction and discussion passages, and updates affiliations and publication text. The major change concerns explanatory depth and document organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds distinct displays for report-generation comparisons, the separate SLAKE evaluation, and pathology frequencies in Tables 3–5. Figure 2 changes its CXR images, overlays, and illustrative outputs. Tables 1–2 gain explicit accuracy units, while Figures 1, 3, and 4 are substantially retained. Together these significantly expand the visual evidence presented.

improvement.justification: v1 provides limited evidence beyond question answering and omits the operative system prompt. v2 adds evaluation of report generation, explicitly discusses its weaker macro-F1 performance, and supplies substantial execution, prompt, and benchmark-construction details. These address important gaps in empirical support and reproducibility. Literature-sourced comparator scores and the continued absence of controlled ablations and uncertainty estimates limit, but do not outweigh, those gains.
